summary: A lake-locked form of Atlantic salmon known regionally as ouananiche, prized for acrobatic jumps and hard runs — a niche fishery limited to specific designated lakes in NB (e.g. Tetagouche, Loch Lomond, Grand, Oromocto) and NS (Grand Lake, Halifax County area), fished from spring open water into fall.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Landlocked salmon are genetically the same species as sea-run Atlantic salmon (*Salmo salar*) — there are no physical differences between the two forms. What differs is life history: instead of migrating to sea, landlocked populations complete their entire life cycle in freshwater, typically using a lake to feed and grow before returning to a connected river or stream to spawn. In Quebec and parts of Atlantic Canada, this form is traditionally known as **ouananiche**.

Landlocked salmon are fall spawners, and adults prefer clear, cold lakes with summer surface temperatures topping out around 21-24°C (70-75°F); as lakes warm through summer, fish move from the relatively warm surface layer down into cooler deep water. They can grow to 50-85 cm where a lake's forage base includes smelt or similar baitfish, while populations relying mainly on insects tend to stay smaller (10-30 cm).

Once hooked, landlocked salmon are known for acrobatic jumps and strong, fast runs — the trait behind the old nickname 'leaping landlocked.'

sources.label: Maine Dept. of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife — Landlocked Salmon Species Information
Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences — Life-History Variability and Conservation Status of Landlocked Atlantic Salmon

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
- **Middle Tetagouche Lake and Upper Tetagouche Lake (Chaleur RFA, NB)** — named designated waters for landlocked salmon angling under NB's fish regulations.
- **Loch Lomond, Grand Lake, and Oromocto Lake (Lower Saint John RFA, NB)** — a cluster of designated landlocked salmon lakes near Saint John.
- **Grand Lake (Halifax County, NS)** — carries a landlocked salmon fishery under Nova Scotia's angling regulations, with extended-season / reduced-limit rules applying October through March.
- Note: Nova Scotia's much larger **Lake Ainslie** (headwaters of the Margaree River, Cape Breton) is known primarily for brook trout, white perch, and gaspereau — it is not established as an ouananiche fishery in the sources checked for this guide, despite sometimes being mentioned alongside landlocked salmon waters. Confirm any specific lake against the current NB Fish Regulations Summary or NS Anglers' Handbook before planning a trip, since landlocked salmon are only legal to angle for in specifically designated waters.

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md:
### New Brunswick
General landlocked salmon season runs roughly **May 1 – September 30** in designated lakes, with most RFAs otherwise prohibiting landlocked salmon angling entirely outside the named waters.

### Nova Scotia
Most designated landlocked salmon lakes are open **April 1 – September 30**, with some waters (e.g. Goose Harbour Lake) open year-round. Grand Lake and similar extended-season waters typically drop to a reduced catch limit from October through March.

In spring, fish sit near the surface where water has warmed fastest; through summer they push down into cooler, deeper water as the surface heats up, so early and late season generally means shallower, more accessible fish.

sources.label: Nova Scotia Anglers' Handbook and 2026 Summary of Regulations

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Fly rod | 6-7 wt, floating line for surface/near-surface fish in spring; sink-tip or full-sink line to reach deeper fish as the season warms. |
| Spinning rod | Medium spinning rod capable of casting small-to-medium spoons and handling a fast-running, jumping fish. |
| Flies/lures | Streamers imitating smelt or other baitfish, small spoons and inline spinners trolled or cast along drop-offs. |
| Extras | Landing net (a jumping fish at boat-side is often lost without one), drag set appropriately loose for sudden runs. |

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
**Spring surface fishing:** work streamers or small spoons along shorelines and points where fish are holding in the warmer surface layer — early morning and evening are prime, similar to trout behaviour.

**Summer depth fishing:** as lakes stratify, target the thermocline or deeper structure with a sink-tip line or by trolling a spoon/streamer at depth — fish follow cooler water down and won't be found shallow in the heat of the day.

**Fighting the fish:** keep your rod tip up and be ready for immediate, often repeated jumps right after the hookset — a controlled drag and quick reactions land more fish than trying to muscle a leaping landlocked salmon back to the boat.

**Surface feeding:** landlocked salmon will rise to take insects off the surface much like a trout, so a well-placed dry fly or small popper during a hatch can also produce, especially on calm evenings.

sources.label: Orvis News — Fish Facts: Landlocked Salmon (Salmo salar sebago)

sections.heading: Handling & Release
sections.body_md:
- Land fish promptly — extended fights in warmer summer surface water raise release mortality risk, similar to sea-run salmon.
- Use a net to control a jumping fish boat-side rather than trying to hand-land it, which often results in a lost hook or a dropped fish that's already exhausted.
- Wet hands before handling, support horizontally, and minimize air exposure for any fish you plan to release, including those over the maximum retention size.
- Nova Scotia enforces an upper release size on landlocked salmon (commonly a maximum around 63 cm, all larger fish released) in addition to a legal minimum — check the current Anglers' Handbook for the exact figures on your lake.

sources.label: Nova Scotia Anglers' Handbook and 2026 Summary of Regulations

sections.heading: Conservation & Consumption Notes
sections.body_md: Landlocked salmon populations are limited to specific lake systems and are managed more conservatively than typical stocked trout — this shows up as low daily bag limits (1-2 fish), minimum size limits, and in Nova Scotia's case a maximum release size designed to protect the largest, most fecund breeding fish. Fish only the specifically designated waters listed in the current provincial regulations; landlocked salmon angling is prohibited by default everywhere else. No region-specific mercury or consumption advisory for landlocked salmon turned up in current provincial sources for this guide.

variants.name: Sea-Run Atlantic Salmon
variants.how_to_tell: Genetically identical to landlocked salmon — same species, no physical differences between the two forms. What differs is life history: sea-run fish migrate to the ocean to feed and grow before returning to their natal river, while landlocked fish complete their entire life cycle using a lake instead of the ocean.
variants.where_found: Sea-run fish are found in open river systems like the Miramichi (NB) and Margaree (NS); landlocked fish are confined to the specific designated lakes covered by this entry.
variants.notes: Completely different regulations apply. Sea-run Atlantic salmon retention is prohibited region-wide (catch-and-release only), while landlocked salmon in designated lakes may be retained within posted bag and size limits. Fishing a designated landlocked lake does not give you any exemption to keep a sea-run fish, and vice versa.

variants.name: Brown Trout
variants.how_to_tell: Landlocked salmon have a slightly forked tail with a thin caudal peduncle, a maxillary (upper jaw) that does not extend much past the eye, and a darker adipose fin with little to no spotting. Brown trout have a nearly square tail with a thicker peduncle, a maxillary that often extends slightly past the eye, more numerous reddish spots overall, and a larger adipose fin that's often orange-tinged with visible spots. Post-spawn male landlocked salmon can turn dark and golden in late fall, making them look especially like a brown trout at first glance.
variants.where_found: Any designated landlocked salmon lake that also holds brown trout — check the current NB/NS regulations for which specific lakes carry both species.
variants.notes: Worth checking carefully where bag limits or size rules differ between the two species in the same lake.
